1. Implementation

The document has been created and approved by the General Assembly of 09.11.2024.
The document and its rules have been implemented since the 2025 season.

2. Definition

Side-pivoting visored Bascinets are helmets with movable visors attached to the dome with pivots at
the temples, in contrast to center-mounted hinges on the forehead. This type of helmet was very
popular in Western Europe from 1350 to 1450. Such helmets are designed to be worn as primary head
protection, and the design of the visor is made to deflect strikes.

Side-pivoting visored Bascinets use a solid metal visor to protect the face, attached on the sides by
pivots.

Side-pivoting visored Bascinets were used from the early 14th century to 1450 across all of Western
Europe. The shape of the visor will evolve throughout time.

3. Historical Sources and Datation

3.1. 14th Century Sugarloaf Helmets

Sugarloaf helmets are one of the earliest types of Side-pivoting visored Bascinets. It appeared at the
beginning of the 14th century and includes a solid chin protection, derived from Great helms design.

Sugarloaf helmets are Approved for 14th century armors.
Sugarloaf helmets are Denied for Transitional and 15th century armors.

BL Royal 6 E IX Address in verse to Robert of Anjou, King of Naples - 1335/1340 - Italy

3.2. Transitional Style Helmets

In the middle of the 14th century, Bascinets with a side-pivoting visor began to be depicted in
miniatures and art. They include a longer visor with no chin plate and will represent the majority of
helmets until the middle of the 15th century.

Transitional style helmets are Approved for 14th century and Transitional armors.
Transitional style helmets are Denied for 15th century armors.

3.3. 15th century Style Helmets

At the edge of the 15th century, an evolution of previous Bascinets was developed. The great Bascinet
encompasses an increased neck protection that makes it very safe. Some extant artifacts are
displayed in museums.

pages.text:
4. Requirements

4.1. General Requirements
Reproductions must closely resemble the appearance and proportions of a Side-pivoting Bascinet
source.

Any metal part of the helmet must conform to the “Armors and Weapons Aesthetics and Decorations”
document.

Any textile or leather part of the helmet must conform to the “Textiles and Leather” document.

4.2. Visor

The visor must not be too long or too short, it must conform to the proportions of historical sources.
The pivots must be reproduced as per historical sources.
It is permitted to weld the visor down. A welded visor must resemble a functional removable visor.

It is permitted to add metal plates to protect the throat. Such a plate must be strong enough to endure
full-contact fighting and must be concealed under the aventail.

A leather strap can be used to secure the visor.

Breath holes should be round and must not exceed a diameter of 10 mm. Breath holes must not be so
numerous that they compromise the helm’s structural integrity. It is acceptable to mirror breath holes to
both sides.

Breath holes of other shapes must be documented by historical sources to be permitted.

4.3. Eye slots

Eye slots should resemble sources for the visor.
Eye slots should not exceed 25 mm tall to prevent any injury.

Side-pivoting visored Bascinets with historical evidence of externally riveted Eye bars can add up to
two (2) externally riveted eye bars per eye slot.

Helmets that are currently documented with externally riveted Eye bars are Sugarloaf and Romance of
Alexander.

Side-pivoting visored Bascinets with two (2) Eye slots are permitted to add up to two (2) safety Eye
bars per Eye slot.

Side-pivoting visored Bascinets with a single Eye slot are permitted to add up to five (5) safety Eye
bars: one (1) in the middle and two (2) on each side.

BL Royal 20 C VII
Chroniques de France ou de St Denis -

Eye bars must conform to the “Eye bars” document.

4.4. Aventail
Side-pivoting visored Bascinets must be worn with chainmail Aventails, fabric Aventails, or scales
Aventails.
Aventails must conform to the “Aventails” document.

Aventails must be attached to the Bascinet by a system of leather and vervelles, or sewn to the edges
of the helmet.

Chainmail Aventail must be fastened down to the edge of a padded pelerine, attached to the helmet
liner.

Scales and fabric Aventails are recommended to be fastened down to the edge of a padded pelerine,
attached to the helmet liner.

Any additional protective plates covering the cervical spine should be hidden under the Aventail.

4.5. Others

Side-pivoting visored Bascinets may be decorated in the spirit of medieval styles, such as an orle,
torse, decorated aventails (with copper/brass chainmail rings), vervelle covers, coat of arms badges,
etc.

Such decoration must be made in coherence with historical sources.
Using modern and/or offensive imagery and slogans is prohibited as part of decorations or heraldry.
